scene: Child: (playing with toys at the table behind while a lady is standing nearby)
Parent: (sitting at the small table, interacting with the tablet)
Parent: "They might fall off now because it's so tall. [inaudible 00:00:12]."
Child: (still at the back table, stacking toys)
Parent: (sitting at the small table, now with a finger on her face)
Parent: "[foreign language 00:00:18]."
Parent: "I'm doing [inaudible 00:00:31]."
Parent: "Okay. And we have to use that two Go Pros."
Child: (moves to small table, sitting beside the parent, and using the tablet)
Parent: (looking at the child's interaction with the tablet)
Parent: "No, not yet."
Child: (continues using the tablet, looking at the screen)
Parent: (sitting beside the child, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Okay. He's on his [inaudible 00:00:41] spirit tablet today."
Child: (engaged with the tablet)
Parent: (sitting beside the child, watching)
Parent: "Oh, that good?"
Child: (looking at the tablet screen, holding the tablet)
Parent: Yeah, I think that's good because you see the bright light flashing and you can start anytime that you want.
Child: (still looking at the tablet screen)
Child: (continues to interact with the tablet)
Parent: Okay.
Child: Okay.
Child: (adjusting the tablet slightly in their hands)
Parent: Click on.
Child: (clicks on the tablet screen)
Child: (the tablet screen appears to change, child looks down at the screen)
Parent: Oops.
Child: (leans in closer to the tablet)
Child: (seated, looking at the tablet)
Parent: (places arm around the child's shoulder, looking at the tablet) "[foreign language 00:01:09]."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, finger on the screen)
Parent: "[foreign language 00:01:21]."
Child: (engaged with the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the screen) "John needs to be super dangerous or dangerous."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: (still pointing at the screen)
Child: (sitting beside the parent, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Let's not be dangerous. What do you think? Oh, here's [foreign language 00:01:41]."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Child: (sitting beside the parent, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "[foreign language 00:01:43]."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Child: (sitting beside the parent, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Oh oh!"
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Child: (sitting beside the parent, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Oh, [foreign language 00:01:48]."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Child: (sitting beside the parent, interacting with the tablet by touching it)
Parent: "The long slow story."
Child: (continues interacting with the tablet, looking focused)
Child: (engaged, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Long story? [foreign language 00:02:08]"
Child: (continues to look at the tablet, interested)

Parent: "We were all sitting around the big kitchen table. It was Saturday morning. Pancake morning! Mom was squeezing oranges for juice and Henry and I were betting on how many pancakes we each could eat and Grandpa was doing the flipping."
Child: (listening attentively, looks up at the parent briefly)
Parent: "How many pancakes can you eat? Nice."
Child: (leans in closer to the tablet, looking at the screen carefully)

Parent: "Seconds later. Something flew through the air, headed toward the kitchen ceiling and landed right on Henry. After we realized that the flying object was only a pancake, we all laughed, even Grandpa. Breakfast continued, quite uneventful. All the other pancakes landed in the pan and all of them were eaten. Even the one that landed on Henry. That night touched off by the pancake incident at breakfast, Grandpa told us the best tall tale bedtime story he had ever told. Across an ocean over lots of huge bumpy mountains across the three hot deserts and one smaller ocean, there laid tiny town of Chewandswallow."
Child: (leans forward, looks at the parent for a second, then back at the tablet)
Parent: "Where is it?"
Child: (pointing at the tablet, engaged in the story)
Child: (leaning in close to the tablet, pointing)
Parent: I think it's here.
Child: (looks towards the screen, nodding)
Parent: Oh, I see it.
Child: (sits back, holding a toy)

Parent: And that looks like far away. In most ways it was very much like any other tiny town. You had a main street lined with stores, houses with trees and gardens around them, the school house, about 300 people and some assorted cats and dogs. But there were no food stores in the town of Chewandswallow. They didn't need any. The sky supplied all the food they could possibly want.
Child: (looks puzzled, pointing at the screen)
Parent: What?
Child: (continues looking at the screen)
Parent: It seems like the food falls out of the sky. Shall we read on? That looks a bit weird.
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: How do you get ice cream?
Child: (holding up one hand, thinking)
Parent: Do you think that only happens in winter?
Child: (smiling, looking excited)
Parent: You're like, "Can I have ice cream?" And it just falls to the ground.
Child: (hand on chin, appearing to consider this)
Parent: What if it's warm though that day? Do you think it would still be frozen by the time it gets down?
Child: (raising hand upwards enthusiastically)
Parent: It has to go through the sun.
Child: (leaning towards the tablet, attentive)
Parent: "Let's see what they get from the sky."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "The only thing that was really different about Chewandswallow was its weather. It came three times a day. At breakfast, lunch, and dinner, everything that everyone ate came from the sky."
Child: (leans closer to the tablet, engaged)

Parent: "Oh, Leo. Wow! Whatever the weather served, that was what they ate. But it never rained rain. It never snowed snow and it never blew just wind. It rained things like soup and juice. It snowed mashed potatoes and green peas and sometimes the wind blew in storms of hamburgers."
Child: (looks up at the parent, curious)
Parent: "Do you think the soup and the juice would come at the same time, or would it be a little bit later and you would have to catch two different things?"
Child: "No, no, no."
Parent: "What do you think?"
Child: (leans in towards the tablet again, thoughtful)
Parent: "The people could watch the weather report on television in the morning and they would even hear a prediction for the next day's food."
Child: (points at the tablet, excited)

Parent: "Wow. When the townspeople went outside, they carried their plates, cups, glasses, forks, spoons, knives, and napkins with them. That way they would always be prepared for any kind of weather. If there were leftovers, and there usually were, the people took them home and put them in their refrigerators in case they got hungry between meals. The menu varied. By the time they woke up in the morning, breakfast was coming down. After a brief shower of orange juice, low clouds of sunny-side-up eggs moved in, followed by pieces of toast. Butter and jelly sprinkled down for the toast, and most of the time it rained milk afterwards."
Child: (ponders, then looks at the parent)
Parent: "Do you think your clothes would get really dirty if you go outside?"
Child: (looking at the book on the tablet)
Parent: Uh huh!
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)

Parent: (pointing at the tablet) For lunch one day frankfurters already in their rolls blew in from the Northwest at about five miles an hour. There were mustard clouds nearby. Then the wind shifted to the East and brought in baked beans. A drizzle of soda finished off the meal.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, focused on the story)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) Oh look, the restaurants don't have roofs, so it just comes inside.
Child: (glances up briefly, then looks back at the tablet with interest)
Child: (raises hand, points at the tablet, and smiles) Because for the food!
Parent: (smiles and looks at the child, then back at the tablet)

Parent: (pointing at the tablet) Dinner one night consisted of lamb chops becoming heavy at times with occasional ketchup. Periods of peas and baked potatoes were followed by gradual clearing with a wonderful jello setting in the West.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, appears engaged with the story)
Child: (looks at the tablet screen with curiosity)
Parent: What's that?
Child: I don't know.
Parent: (points at the screen) Do you think that's the garbage people cleaning up after the weather comes through?
Child: (starts to point at the screen)

Parent: The sanitation department of Chewandswallow had a rather unusual job for a sanitation department. It had to remove the food that fell on the houses and sidewalks and lawns. The workers cleaned things up after every meal and fed all the dogs and cats. Then they emptied some of it into the surrounding oceans for the fish and turtles and whales to eat.
Child: (points at the screen again) Did he eat this?
Parent: (shakes head) No.
Parent: The rest of the food was put back into the earth so that the soil would be richer for the people's flower gardens.
Child: (looking at the tablet screen, listening attentively)
Parent: "Life for the townspeople was delicious until the weather took a turn for the worst."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet screen)
Parent: "Spaghetti Ties Up Town." (points at the screen)
Child: (still focused on the tablet screen)

Parent: "One day there was nothing but Gorgonzola cheese all day long. The next day there was only broccoli, all over cooked. And the next day there was Brussels sprouts and peanut butter with mayonnaise." (pointing again at the screen)
Child: (still engaged with the tablet screen, no visible reaction)
Parent: "Are they happy with that?"
Child: (still paying attention to the screen)
Parent: "No."
Child: (looking at the tablet with the parent)
Parent: Another day there was a pea soup fog. No one could see where they were going and they could barely find the rest of the meal that got stuck in the fog.
Child: (continues to look at the tablet)
Parent: Do you know what a fog is?
Child: (shakes head) No.
Parent: It's a low-hanging cloud and then you can't see anything else.
Child: (still looking at the tablet, nodding slightly)
Parent: The food was getting larger and larger and so were the portions. The people were getting frightened as violent storms blew up frequently. Awful things were happening.
Child: (eyes widen slightly, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: Wow. What is that?
Child: (points at the tablet) Pancake.
Parent: A pancake that covers an entire house? What do they have to do? What do they have to do with it?
Child: (continues to look at the tablet intensely, visibly intrigued)
Child: (looking at the tablet screen)
Parent: Big helicopters.
Child: (continuing to look at the tablet screen)

Parent: One Tuesday there was a hurricane of bread and rolls all day long and into the night. There were soft rolls and hard rolls, some with seeds and some without. There was white bread and rye, and whole wheat toast. Some of it was larger than they had ever seen bread and rolls before. It was a terrible day. Everyone had to stay indoors. Roofs were damaged and the sanitation department was beside itself. The mess took the workers four days to clean up and the sea was full of floating rolls.
Child: (still looking at the tablet screen)
Parent: Wow. Do you think a lot of animals would come to eat all the food?
Child: (nodding or softly replying "Yeah")
Parent: To help out, the people piled up as much bread as they could in their backyards. The birds picked at it a bit, but just stayed there and it got staler and staler.
Child: (both looking at the tablet, following along with the reading)
Parent: Know what stale means?
Child: No.
Parent: It means old bread or old food.
Child: (still focused on the tablet, listening)

Parent: There was a storm of pancakes one morning and a downpour of maple syrup that nearly flooded the town. A huge pancake covered the school. No one could get it off because of it's weight, so they had to close the school.
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: Is that good or bad?
Child: Bad.
Parent: Bad? Because a pancake falls on the school and you can't go to school?
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Lunch one day, brought 15 inch drifts of cream cheese and jelly sandwiches. Everyone ate themselves sick and the day ended with a stomach ache. There was an awful salt and pepper wind accompanied by an even worse tomato tornado. People were sneezing themselves silly and running to avoid the tomatoes. The town was a mess. There were seeds and pulp everywhere."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: "What is that?" (points to the tablet) "Gets scooped up in his bathtub."
Child: (follows the parent’s finger on the tablet)

Parent: "The sanitation department gave up. The job was too big. Everyone feared for their lives. They couldn't go outside most of the time. Many houses had been badly damaged by giant meatballs. Stores were boarded up and there was no more school for the children. So a decision was made to abandon the town of Chewandswallow. It was a matter of survival. The people glued together the giant pieces of stale bread, sandwich style with peanut butter."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "What did they do?"
Child: (turns slightly towards the parent)
Parent: "They made boats."
Child: (looking back at the tablet)
Parent: "They're making boats."
Child: (looking at the tablet screen and listening to the story)

Parent: (reading from the tablet) "Took the absolute necessities with them and set sail on their rafts for a new land. After being afloat for a week, they finally reached a small coastal town, which welcomed them. The bread had held up surprisingly well enough for them to build temporary houses for themselves out of it."
Child: (looks up and exclaims) "Oh! Bread houses!"

Parent: (continues reading) "The children began school again and the adults all tried to find places for themselves in the new land. The biggest change they had to make was getting used to buying food at a supermarket. They found it odd that the food was kept on shelves, packaged in boxes, cans, and bottles. Meat that had to be cooked was kept in large refrigerators. Nothing came down from the sky except rain and snow. The clouds above their heads were not made of fried eggs. No one ever got hit by a hamburger again and nobody dared to go back to Chewandswallow to find out what had happened to it. They were too afraid."
Child: (continues to listen attentively and looks at the tablet screen)

Parent: (continues reading) "Henry and I were awake until the very end of Grandpa's story. I remember his goodnight kiss. The next morning we woke up to see snow falling outside our window. We ran downstairs for breakfast and ate it a little faster than usual so we could go sledding with Grandpa. It's funny, but even as we were sliding down the hill, we thought we saw a giant pat of butter at the top and we could almost smell mashed potatoes."
Child: (looks at the tablet screen and points) "What are they doing?"
Parent: (looks closely at the screen with the child for a moment, then continues reading)
Child: (pointing at the tablet, engaged in the story)
Parent: "Getting food from the sky."
Child: (continues to point at the tablet)
Parent: "Will I read you a short story? These are long stories."
Child: (looking at the tablet, seems curious)
Parent: "They're all long stories. These are short stories. Can I turn it off now?"
Child: (looks at parent, appears to be considering)
Parent: (looking at the child, waiting for a response)
Child: "Sure. Ready?"
Parent: (smiling, getting ready to read)
Parent: (reading from the tablet) "Officer Buckle knew more safety tips than anyone else in Napville. Every time he thought of a new one, he thumb tacked it to his bulletin board."
Child: (sitting attentively, listening to the story)
Parent: (points to the tablet) "Safety tip number 77 - never stand on a swivel chair."
Child: "What is a swivel chair? Is that one of these that can turn around?"
Parent: "Yeah."
Child: (nodding, understanding the explanation)
Parent: (continuing to read) "Officer Buckle shared his safety tips with the students at Napville school. Nobody ever listened. Sometimes there was snoring."
Child: (laughs softly, enjoying the story)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: Would you listen to those safety tips? Yeah? Cool.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Child: (eagerly gazing at the tablet)
Parent: Afterwards it was business as usual. Mr Topple, the principal, took down the welcome banner. "Never stand on a swivel chair," said officer Buckle, but Mrs Topple didn't hear him.
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: Oh, what was she doing?
Child: (looking at the tablet, leaning in)
Child: (looking at the tablet, hands close together)
Parent: Standing on one.
Child: (continues to look at the tablet)
Child: (adjusting his gloves)

Parent: Then one day Napville's police department bought a police dog named Gloria. When it was time for officer Buckle to give the safety speech at the school, Gloria went along. "Children, this is Gloria," announced officer Buckle. "Gloria obeys my commands." "Gloria sit." And Gloria sat. Officer Buckle gave safety tip number one - keep your shoelaces tied. The children sat up and stared.
Child: (still adjusting gloves, looking at the tablet)
Child: (focused on his gloves)
Parent: What's the dog doing? Helping?
Child: (continuing to look at his gloves)
Child: (gazing at the tablet, slightly adjusting gloves)

Parent: Officer Buckle checked to see if Gloria was sitting at attention and she was. "Safety tip number two," said officer Buckle, "Always wipe up spills before someone slips and falls." The children's eyes popped.
Child: (still focused on his gloves)
Child: (looking at the parent briefly)
Parent: Why do you think that is? What's the dog doing?
Child: (slight pause) Smelling.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet)
Child: (continues to look at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, hands near face)
Parent: "Officer Buckle checked on Gloria again. 'Good dog,' he said. Officer Buckle thought of a safety tip he had discovered that morning."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, hands near face)
Parent: "Oh look. He has a patch."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, hands near face)
Parent: "'Never leave a thumbtack where you might sit on it.'"
Child: (remains focused on the tablet, hands near face)
Parent: "What does the dog do?"
Child: "Sit on it?"

Parent: (smiling) "The audience roared. Officer Buckle grinned. He said the rest of the tips with plenty of expression. The children clapped their hands and cheered. Some of them laughed until they cried. Officer Buckle was surprised. He had never noticed how funny safety tips could be. After this safety speech, there wasn't a single accident. The next day, an enormous envelope arrived at the police station. It was stuffed with thank you letters from the students at Napville school."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) Do you want me to read one of the letters?
Child: (looking at the tablet) Uh huh.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) "Dear Gloria and officer Buckle. Thanks for coming to our school. You are nice. Your friend George."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) Every letter had a drawing of Gloria on it. Officer Buckle thought the drawings showed a lot of imagination.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: Is it imagination or did the kids see the dog do all these things?
Child: (looking at the tablet) See the dog do all the things.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) "Dear Gloria and officer Buckle. Thanks for coming to our school. You are nice. Your friend George."
Child: That's the letter we just saw.
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: (pointing at the tablet) His favorite letter was written on a star-shaped piece of paper. It said, "You and Gloria make a good team. Your friend Claire. P.S. I always wear a crash helmet - safety tip number seven."
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: (pointing at the tablet) Officer Buckle was thumb-tacking Claire's letter to his bulletin board, when the phone started ringing. Grade schools, high schools and daycare centers were calling about the safety speech. "Officer Buckle," they said, "Our students want to hear your safety tips and please bring along that police dog. Officer Buckle told his safety tips to 313 schools. Everywhere he and Gloria went, children sat up and listened. At every speech officer Buckle took Gloria out for ice cream. Officer Buckle loved having a buddy."
Child: (looking at the tablet) What is the dog doing here?

Parent: (pointing at the tablet) Then one day, television news, Teen, videotaped officer Buckle in the State college auditorium. When he finished safety tip number 99 - do not go swimming during electrical storms.
Child: What does the dog do?
Parent: I don't know.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: The students jumped to their feet and applauded.
Child: Maybe he's showing what happens to you when you go swimming during an electrical storm. You get all fuzzy.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) "Bravo. Bravo," they cheered. Officer Buckle bowed again and again. That night, officer Buckle watched himself on the 10 o’clock news.
Child: What do you think is going to be surprised about?
Parent: The dog.
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: (pointing at the tablet) The next day, the principal of Napville school telephoned the police station. "Good morning, officer Buckle. It’s time for our safety speech." Officer Buckle frowned. "I'm not giving any more speeches. Nobody looks at me anyway." "Oh," said Mrs. Topple. "Well, how about Gloria? Could she come?" Someone else from the police station gave Gloria a ride to the school. Gloria sat on stage looking lonely. Then she fell asleep. So did the audience. After Gloria left, Napville school had its biggest accident ever. The next morning, a pile of letters arrived at the police station. Every letter had a drawing of the accident. Officer Buckle was shocked. At the bottom of the pile was a note written on a paper star. Officer Buckle smiled. The note said, "It started with a puddle of banana pudding, splat splatter splosh. Everyone slipped and smacked into Mrs. Topple who screamed and let go of her hammer."
Child: While she’s standing on the chair.
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: (pointing at the tablet) Gloria gave officer Buckle a big kiss on the nose. Officer Buckle gave Gloria a nice pat on the back. Then officer Buckle thought of his best safety tip yet. "Gloria missed you yesterday. Your friend Claire. Don't worry. I was wearing my helmet. Safety tip number seven."
Child: (looking at the tablet) Safety tip number 101 – always stick with your buddy.
Child: (looking at the tablet) Oh, I think these are different safety tips.
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) Never play alone in the car.
Child: Alone.
Parent: Oh, what is this? Stay away from guns is it? Yep.
Child: (looking at the tablet) Buckle your seatbelt.
Child: (looking at the tablet) How about this one?
Parent: Look both ways before you cross the street.
Child: (looking at the tablet) That’s the last page.
Parent: I think story time is up.
Child: Okay.
Parent: Thank you very much.
Child: (starts getting up from the chair)
Parent: (starts taking off headgear) Take this off.
Child: (raises hands up)
Parent: And I can take these off.
